extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, Fellows of the Royal Society, experimental scientists and natural historians (17th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and reviewing early modern experimental natural philosophy: laboratory pneumatic and chemical experiments and natural history monographs, with emphasis on careful observation, apparatus, and organization of descriptive works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of exposure to air in solution experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe and control access of the outward air to reaction vessels; opening or closing the stopper produces rapid and repeatable colour changes in solutions (e.g., dark brown → green → clear) within minutes to hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments report repeatedly that unstopping lets air in and the upper surface quickly acquires colour which penetrates; resealing often causes the tincture to fade again over days. Timing of opening/closing and observation intervals (minutes, hours, days) are critical to the reported phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid agitation to prevent confounding precipitates
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not shake vessels when observing colour/tincture changes, because agitation might raise fine powder that could be mistaken for restored colour by suspended precipitate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author explicitly: 'In most of these experiments I forbore to shake the glass, lest it should be suspected, that the agitation of the liquor might have raised some little fine powder, that might have been supposed... to restore it to its former colour.' Use still conditions to avoid this confound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mercurial gauge to detect changes in the 'spring' or pressure of air
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a mercurial gauge in sealed vessels to record compressive or expansive effects on the confined air as a measurable depression or ascent of mercury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed phenomena: sustained descent of mercury in sealed leg over days indicates weakening of the spring of the included air; brisk bubbles/vapour production compresses air transiently; prolonged actions produce durable changes. Record gauge marks and compare before/after and with controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ hermetic sealing and careful sealing technique for pneumatic experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Achieve and verify airtight seals between receiver and cover (e.g., well-ground edges, wetted lamb's skin, close-fitting glass-plate) to produce reliable vacua and to prevent spurious ingress of air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note: even a small defect (a hail-shot of lead) prevented exact application and allowed freer egress/ingress of air. Use layered coverings and confirm tight fit before pumping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use paired receivers and pumps for generation and measurement of small quantities of air
rubrics_metrics.description: Place small exhausted receiver inside a larger one and use the air-pump to create and compare vacua, enabling estimation of air formed within the small receiver by observing its ability to lift under the larger receiver's pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure described: exhaust both, then allow the larger receiver's air to press on the small one; observe whether the small receiver later raises, indicating air formation; repeatably compare capacity of small vs large receiver to detect small amounts of formed air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and record effects of vacuum on plant parts (leaves vs roots) over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Place parts of a plant in vacuo while other parts remain in air or water and document morphological and physiological responses (drops forming on leaves, bubbles from roots, withering, root elongation) over days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: leaves in vacuo produced drops; roots in vacuo produced bubbles; leaves not immediately withered though not grown; plants kept longer in vacuo were spoiled. Record timing (minutes, hours, days) and compare morphological details (colour change, smell, growth rate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use controls comparing water purged of air versus common water
rubrics_metrics.description: Test vegetation by placing identical plant cuttings in water from which air has been removed and in ordinary (air-containing) water, and compare days-to-rooting, number and length of roots, and subsequent growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported results: twig in common water shot roots in ~6 days and had many roots; twig in degassed water sometimes delayed to 10 days, or exhibited fewer/longer single roots. Repeat experiments to check variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation criterion: air in water aids vegetation
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclude from comparative vacuum and purged-water experiments that the air mixed in common water serves for vegetation and affects the vigor and multiplicity of root growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors report that although some repetitions gave variable timing, overall experiments 'confirmed the first opinion, that the air which is mixed in common water serves for vegetation.' Use repeated trials to support the inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design experiments to detect whether water can be forced through plant tissues by pressure differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Configure experiments with parts of a stem in air and parts in vacuo and drench the air-side in water to observe whether water is forced into the plant and appears in the vacuo side (drops or bubbles), thereby testing permeability and the presence/effectiveness of valves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations: sallow produced bubbles and water passed through; buff allowed water but produced no bubbles. Cutting back tender parts enabled droplets to form and fall. Interpret differences as due to tissue firmness/tenderness rather than valves alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and method for natural history monographs: ocular inspection first
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize describing species 'from ocular inspection'; where the author/editor could not see specimens, borrow descriptions 'from the best writers' rather than collecting indiscriminately from all published accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review of Willughby: 'The design of this work is not to give pandects of birds, or to collect indiscriminately what has been already published... but to illustrate and set in order the history of birds, partly by describing the birds themselves from ocular inspection, partly by borrowing the description of those... which the author and editor themselves could not get a sight [of].'

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize accurate description, natural classification, and lifelike illustration
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide accurate descriptions and reduce species to natural classes; illustrate with 'Iconibus elegantissimis et Vivarum Avium simillimis' (very elegant and lifelike engraved images).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The work is praised for describing 'Aves omnes hactenus cognitae, in methodum naturis suis convenientem redactae' and for being 'accurate' with elegant and lifelike plates; include catalogues of resident and migratory species and divisions of taxa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational completeness for an ornithological treatise
rubrics_metrics.description: Structurally divide the work into parts treating (1) birds in general (external/internal parts, generation, age, moult, classification), (2) land-fowl (subdivisions by beak/claw form and habits), and (3) water-fowl (further subdivisions by lifestyle and morphology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review enumerates contents: treatment of pectoral muscles, brain differences, generation (egg/ovum as 'uterus expositus'), divisions into classes, and catalogues of resident and migratory birds. A thorough monograph should cover anatomy, behavior, reproduction, diet, and distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include behavioural, ecological, and practical-natural history notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Report on behaviour (conjugal life, flight patterns), diet tolerances, medicinal uses, and human uses/practices (e.g., methods for capons to brood, use of pigeons for carrying letters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review notes many such particulars as valuable: examples of unusual diets without harm, medicinal recipes, and practical husbandry tips; inclusion of such observations strengthens the natural-history utility of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopic and comparative anatomical description of plant trunks
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe trunks both as seen by the naked eye (different trunk types) and under a microscope (bark: skin, parenchyma, vessels; wood: parenchyma and vessels; pith composed of parenchyma and sap-vessels), and discuss varieties of vessel types (sap, air, lactiferous, resiniferous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grew's work is commended for accurate naked-eye and microscopic descriptions, asserting analogies between animal and plant vessels, and detailing how different trunks and tissues correspond to functional roles in vegetation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize vegetation explanation under explicit thematic heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain vegetation on the basis of anatomy under specific heads: (1) motion and course of the sap, (2) motion of the air, (3) structure of parts, (4) generation of liquors, (5) figuration of trunks, (6) motions of trunks, and (7) nature of trunks as fitted to mechanical uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review lists these seven heads and commends use of anatomical grounding to explain vegetation (e.g., how sap becomes vinous, resinous, oily; causes of tree shapes; why heartwood is durable; grafting conjunctions). Use this explicit organization to cover function and applied consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide practical applications and mechanical explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate anatomical findings to practical and mechanical uses: which woods are soft/hard/tough/durable, why heartwood is most durable, what plants make best tow, and how to recognise successful grafting conjunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grew's second part includes such applied accounts; monographs should connect structure to materials science and horticultural practice where possible.
